expectations.text: Output identifies that the model is missing a by-subject random slope for condition
expectations.evidence: Problem 1 (Critical): Missing random slope for condition — 'Your condition manipulation is within-subjects… it must have a by-subject random slope.'

expectations.text: Output explicitly states or strongly implies that the analysis is NOT defensible as-is — does NOT validate it or describe it as 'broadly fine'
expectations.evidence: 'This doesn't look right, and the issue is significant enough that you shouldn't write it up with this model.' and 'Your t = 2.91 and p = .004 cannot be trusted from this specification.'

expectations.text: Output explains that omitting the by-subject slope inflates Type I error (anti-conservative p-value) for within-subjects effects
expectations.evidence: 'The subject-by-condition interaction variance gets absorbed into the residual, which means the denominator of your test is too small and your t-statistic is too large… the Type I error rate under a random-intercepts-only model can run 2–5× the nominal rate.'

expectations.text: Output references Barr et al. (2013) / Keep It Maximal, OR Schielzeth & Forstmeier (2009), OR explains the Type I inflation mechanism (wrong error term for within-subjects test)
expectations.evidence: Explicitly cites both 'Barr et al., 2013' and 'Schielzeth & Forstmeier, 2009' and also explains the mechanism (residual absorbs slope variance, denominator too small).

expectations.text: Output recommends refitting with a by-subject random slope — e.g. (1 + condition | subject) or equivalent
expectations.evidence: 'What you need at minimum: lmer(rating ~ condition + (1 + condition | subject), data = d)'
